An empirical approach
If we’re interested in one’s overall level of confidence, let’s simply compute mean confidence!




\[
\mathbb{E}\left[C\right] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n C_n = \sum_c P(C=c) c
\]







Pro: high face validity
Con: confounded with Type I performance

title: A measure of metacognitive biasyou can be confident in
text:
meta-\(\Delta\)



Same idea, with two adjustments:


Don’t normalize distances by meta-\(d'\) (Dijkstra et al., 2024)
Take the average of all confidence criteria




\[\begin{align*}
    \textrm{meta-}\Delta_r &= \left|\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\left[\textrm{meta-}c_{2,k}^r\right] - \textrm{meta-}c\right|
\end{align*}\]


\[\begin{align*}
    \textrm{meta-}\Delta_r &= \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \frac{K - k}{K-1}\textrm{dmeta-}c_{2,k}^r
\end{align*}\]

title: A measure of metacognitive biasyou can be confident in
text:
Conclusions
 


Mean confidence is not a valid measure of metacognitive bias
Metacognitive bias seems important, but previous studies are subject to performance confounds
For those already using \(M\)-ratio to quantify metacognitive efficiency, meta-\(\Delta\) provides an independent, unbiased, and highly reliablemeasure of metacognitive bias
